data.title: Consumers' medium- and long-term inflation expectations appear anchored: NY Fed
data.description:
Consumers' outlook for inflation expectations hasn't changed much in the past month, but they still don't see inflation falling to the Federal Reserve's 2% goal anytime soon, according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations.

Their outlook on their current and future household financial situation looked a little brighter. Meanwhile, their expectations on job loss deteriorated, while their perception of finding a job if they needed to improved. 

The median inflation expectation at the one-year-ahead timeframe ticked down 0.1 percentage point to 3.6% in July, while those at the three-year and five-year horizons were unchanged at 3.3% and 3.0%, respectively.

Consumers also appeared more certain about their inflation expectations at the one- and five-year horizons. The median inflation uncertainty at the three-year horizon was unchanged.

Federal Reserve policymakers closely watch inflation expectations in calculating interest rate decisions. If consumers expect inflation to surge in coming years, the policymakers will be more likely to raise rates to tamp down on demand, thereby reducing inflationary pressures.

The mean perceived probability of losing one's job edged up by 0.1 pp to 14.2%, still below the 12-month trailing average of 14.5%. The mean probability that the U.S. employment rate will rise in the year ahead increased by 1.1 pp to 42.8%.

Consumers' confidence in finding a job if they lose their current one, though, rose, with the mean perceived probability of finding a job up 1.3 pp to 46.2%.

On the household finance side, consumers' median expected growth in household income was unchanged at 3.0% in July. The median year-ahead outlook on spending growth ticked down 0.1 pp to 4.9%, slightly below the 12-month trailing average of 5.0%, the New York Fed said.

Still, they appear to be more concerned about keeping up on debt payments.  The median perceived probability of missing a minimum debt payment over the next three months rose 1.2 pp to 12.0%, still below the 12-month trailing average of 12.7%.

data.title: Medical devices ETF nears breakout; here are its top holdings
data.description:
The U.S. Medical Devices ETF (IHI) could be nearing a technical breakout as strength in the broader healthcare sector prompts investors to rotate into lagging industry groups, according to Donovan Jackson of Stock Market Media.

Jackson said medical devices had been one of the weakest areas within healthcare but could also emerge as one of the biggest beneficiaries if artificial intelligence is successfully integrated across the industry.

With the broader healthcare ETF (XLV) on track to end the week at a record high, Jackson said capital could gradually rotate into underperforming healthcare subsectors rather than continue chasing stocks that had already posted strong gains.

A chart shared by Jackson showed IHI forming what he described as a tactical base just below its pivot lows from April. According to the analysis, a move above the $55 level would mark a breakout and open the door for a rally toward the next resistance area near $65, implying a potential upside of nearly 20%.

Jackson said the setup offered investors an opportunity to gain exposure to the healthcare sector without chasing recent winners.

data.title: Lilly, Novo antitrust case over GLP-1s dismissed in Texas
data.description:
A federal judge in Texas has dismissed a lawsuit filed by a compounding pharmacy alleging that Eli Lilly (LLY) and Novo Nordisk (NVO) engaged in antitrust behavior by ​blocking access to customized versions of their blockbuster GLP-1 drugs.

Judge Micaela Alvarez of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas issued the ruling on Thursday against the compounding pharmacy, ​Strive Specialties, in response to requests filed by the pharma giants seeking ​a dismissal.

Strive alleged that Lilly (LLY) and Novo (NVO) infringed on U.S. antitrust law by reaching exclusive partnerships with leading telehealth providers, thus preventing physicians on those platforms from prescribing customized versions of their branded GLP-1s.

Alvarez said Strive failed to prove its antitrust injuries because its compounded GLP-1 drugs don’t operate in the same market as Lilly (LLY) and Novo (NVO)​, whose branded versions Zepbound and Wegovy contain tirzepatide and semaglutide as active ingredients, respectively.

Strive, noting its disappointment with the ruling, told Reuters it was confident of its stance and was weighing options, including plans to file an appeal. 

Indiana-based Lilly (LLY) said, “This meritless claim should have never been brought against Lilly.” The ruling “confirms that companies mass-compounding tirzepatide are violating the law,” the company added.

Its Danish rival, meanwhile, noted that it was “pleased with the court's decision to dismiss all claims against Novo Nordisk.” The company added that it continues to focus on its mission.

data.title: QuinStreet shares surge after strong earnings beat fueled by insurance and home services growth
data.description:
QuinStreet (QNST) shares jumped as much as 37% in the early trading on Friday after the online performance marketing company delivered fourth-quarter results that exceeded Wall Street expectations and pointed to continued momentum across its core verticals.

The company reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.50 for the fiscal fourth quarter, up from $0.25 a year earlier and above the ecpectations of $0.44, as per data compiled by Bloomberg. Revenue climbed 43% year over year to $373.9 million, beating expectations of $359.8 million, while adjusted EBITDA rose 87% to $41.4 million, ahead of estimates of $40.1 million.

Growth was led by strength in QuinStreet’s (QNST) two primary markets. Revenue from Financial Services increased 24% year over year to $232.3 million, while Home Services revenue nearly doubled, rising 98% to $141.6 million.

Adjusted net income reached $29.0 million, compared with $14.7 million a year ago, while adjusted diluted earnings per share improved to $0.50 from $0.25.

Shares have surged around 43% so far this year, outpacing the 12.6% gain of the broader index.

data.title: Earnings could be an early indicator of any degradation in labor market—Richmond Fed's Barkin
data.description:
Earnings could be an early indicator of any possible degradation in the labor market in terms of layoffs, according to Tom Barkin, CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond.

Barkin was speaking in a fireside chat on the economy, leadership, and the evolving role of the Fed before the event hosted by the National Association for Business Economics.

This low hire, low fire trend has been with us for quite some time, according to Barkin. "I think the equilibrium is somewhat self-reinforcing."

"Obviously, it could shift with a downward shift in people's job prospects, and I think the biggest thing I'm watching on that is earnings," he said.

"Corporate earnings are quite strong, and growing nicely in aggregate in multiple sectors, and, you know, you're not going to do a lot of layoffs if you've got strong earnings," said the Federal Open Market Committee's alternate voting member.

Earnings are a buffer against further degradation in the labor market, according to Barkin.

U.S. nonfarm payrolls declined by 23K in July, missing the +88K consensus and erasing the 20K increase in June.

Even more jarring than the July reversal in jobs growth, revisions to the prior two months described a labor market that was significantly weaker than previously thought. June's growth was scaled back by more than half from the initial print of 57K. May's estimate was slashed to +63K from +129K.

The unemployment rate, though, dropped as the labor force participation rate declined again.

To the businesses that he is talking to, the Richmond Fed president is asking questions about compensation pressures right now, not layoffs. "The things about layoffs are they don't just happen; you have to plan a layoff."

For demand, the Richmond Fed prez said credit card spending could be a real-time indicator of demand.

"In the second quarter, when oil prices went up and non-gas spending also went up, you know, that was a good predictor for me of what we saw in the second quarter, which is real PCE. It was very healthy," said Barkin.

Developing... Check back for updates.

data.title: Gold, silver miners stay on Hold rating despite precious metals rally
data.description:
Gold and silver prices extended their rally this week, with spot silver surging toward $65 an ounce and gold futures approaching $4,400 an ounce, as investors piled into precious metals amid strong momentum.

Against that backdrop, Seeking Alpha's Quant Ratings paint a more measured picture for mining stocks, with none of the top-ranked gold and silver names earning a bullish rating.

Below is a list of the top 10 gold and silver stocks screened using Seeking Alpha's Quant Ratings. The ranking is dominated by precious metals miners, with all companies carrying Hold recommendations despite the sharp advance in underlying commodity prices.

Dakota Gold Corp. (DC) leads the list with a Quant Rating of 3.15, narrowly ahead of AngloGold Ashanti plc (AU) at 3.13 and Aura Minerals Inc. (AUGO) at 3.06. The rankings are tightly clustered, with scores ranging from 3.15 at the top to 2.63 for Vista Gold Corp. (VGZ).

Newmont Corporation (NEM), the largest company on the list with a market capitalization of $111.09 billion, ranks fourth with a 3.05 Quant Rating. Hecla Mining Company (HL) is the only silver-focused miner among the top 10, posting a 2.75 rating.

Seeking Alpha's Quant Ratings evaluate stocks across five key quantitative factors, including valuation, growth, profitability, earnings revisions, and momentum. Ratings are assigned on a scale of 1 to 5, with scores of 3.5 or higher considered Bullish, while ratings of 2.5 or below are viewed as Bearish.

data.title: Datadog in the spotlight as Citi says buy the dip
data.description:
• Datadog (DDOG) was in the spotlight on Friday as Citi said investors should buy the dip after it reported better-than-expected results and guidance.
  • “DDOG commendably delivered against a high/raised bar with revs profitably-accelerating 36% YoY on broad-based/balanced strength, as AI-natives (CitiE ~97% YoY) and non-AI-natives (CitiE ~28% YoY) equally prove-out structurally upsurging observability demand,” Citi analyst Fatima Boolani wrote in a note to clients. “AINs accelerating ~28pts QoQ even excluding DDOG's largest 9-figure customer impressed, validating cohort breadth/diversity. Yet, QoQ RPO $-compression, mega customer usage-reduction, and their likely flattish commit-renewal (CitiE) will foment some angst (loosely implying spend tracking ~50% of C2Q's ~$90-95M high-watermark per CitiE). However, we'd emphasize that like C1Q, DDOG only embedding minimum contracted-revs in guide + mgmt's confidence on de-minimis DIY/insourcing risk means heavy prudence with upside usage volatility, offering sustained mid-30+ growth optionality, as GTM/product cadence demonstrably fires on all cylinders business-wide. DDOG is cementing strategic value to consequential AI companies and 'classic' enterprises' AI adoption/modernization initiatives alike—and this unique nexus justifies premium valuation, reinforcing our Buy.”
  • In addition to the reiterated Buy rating, Boolani also raised her price target on Datadog to $305 from $300.

data.title: Arrow Electronics falls 10% despite earnings beat, strong outlook
data.description:
Arrow Electronics (ARW) shares fell about 10% on Friday despite the electronic components distributor reporting second-quarter results that topped Wall Street expectations and issuing an upbeat third-quarter earnings outlook.

The company posted non-GAAP earnings of $5.45/share, beating analyst estimates by $1, while revenue climbed 32% year over year to $10B, exceeding consensus forecasts by about $450M.

Growth was driven by strong demand across both operating segments. Global Components sales rose 39% from a year earlier to $7.37B, while Global Enterprise Computing Solutions revenue increased 14% to $2.63B.

Arrow forecast third-quarter revenue of $9.6B to $10.2B, in line with market expectations, while projecting non-GAAP earnings of $4.83 to $5.03/share, above the consensus estimate of $4.68.

Management said healthy demand across regions and end markets, together with higher-margin value-added offerings and disciplined capital allocation, positions the company for continued profitable growth.

data.title: Full House Resorts targets $30M-$40M annual EBITDA at Chamonix amid plan to close refinancing in Q3
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Full House Resorts (FLL) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "We had a strong quarter of growth led by our two newest properties, American Place and Chamonix" (President, CFO, Treasurer & Director Lewis Fanger). "On a consolidated basis, revenues grew 5.6% in the second quarter and adjusted EBITDA increased 19.5%."
  • "American Place... once again had its best quarter ever" (President Fanger). "Revenues at American Place rose 13.4% to $34.8 million" and "Adjusted property EBITDA... rose by 13.8% to $10.1 million." He added: "In May of 2026, we... reach[ed] $12.7 million" in monthly gaming revenue.
  • "At Chamonix... we launched new, more targeted marketing strategies" (President Fanger). "Those efforts helped revenues rise almost 12% in the quarter" and "Adjusted property EBITDA was approximately break-even for the quarter." He also said the company "added a new casino director" with experience "at Fontainebleau" and "at Wynn in Las Vegas for almost 15 years."
  • "Rising Star was impacted during the quarter by a 42-hour power outage" (President Fanger). "At Silver Slipper, revenues declined slightly... and adjusted property EBITDA slightly improved" as the company continued "eliminat[ing] unprofitable business."
  • "As a result, we are now permitted to operate our Temporary Facility until February of 2029" (President Fanger), after legislative passage and Gaming Board approval; he said the company "hope[s] and believe[s] we can get this done in the third quarter" regarding the refinancing.
  • "Sometimes that masks how well results actually are" (Chief Executive Officer & Director Daniel Lee), citing segment reporting effects, adding: "Rising Star... actually lost $100,000 in the quarter" and "Silver Slipper... did $3.4 million in the same quarter of both years." He also said the West segment moved "from a loss last year of $1.2 million to just under break-even."

Outlook

  • "Our goal is to improve our win per position per day figure of about $175" at Chamonix (President Fanger). "If we can hit the Black Hawk average... that results in roughly $30 million of annual EBITDA" and "If we can get a 15% premium to the Black Hawk average... you approach $40 million of EBITDA," while adding: "We don't expect to be there this year or even fully there next year, but we do expect to make massive improvement over the coming 18 months."
  • "We hope and believe we can get this done in the third quarter" on the refinancing (President Fanger). CEO Lee similarly said, "we expect to get it all done this quarter" and described the process as "a very complex thing we're trying to do."
  • "It's 18 to 24 months" for the permanent American Place build, and "opening in the third quarter of 2028, probably a good guess" (CEO Lee).

Financial Results

  • "Revenues at American Place rose 13.4% to $34.8 million" and "Adjusted property EBITDA... rose... to $10.1 million" (President Fanger).
  • "On a consolidated basis, revenues grew 5.6% in the second quarter and adjusted EBITDA increased 19.5%" (President Fanger).
  • "Adjusted property EBITDA was approximately break-even for the quarter" at Chamonix (President Fanger), while CEO Lee said Chamonix improved by "$1.1 million" and that with certain fees "we probably would have made a little bit of money."
  • "We're running 29% plus margins pretty consistently" at American Place, CEO Lee said, adding this is "after paying rent to the City of $3 million a year, a little north of $3 million a year" and about "$1.5 million a year" for rented kitchens and office space; he and President Fanger pointed to a permanent-facility margin goal of "Mid-30s."
  • "In the month of May, we did $4.4 million of EBITDA on that $12.7 million of gaming revenue" at American Place (President Fanger).

Q&A

  • Jordan Bender, Citizens JMP: asked whether the permanent American Place plan has changed; CEO Lee said, "It's refined it," adding the temporary property is doing "$12 million a month of revenues roughly" and "we've had very little, if any, competitive impact."
  • Bender, Citizens JMP: asked about business interruption insurance from Rising Star’s outage; CEO Lee said, "No," because "you only get business interruption insurance if you have a property damage claim."
  • Will Yager, Craig-Hallum: pressed on financing timing; CEO Lee said, "we're 95% sure we're going to get there" and noted spending "probably $1.5 million" on plans and civil work, while warning, "if we ran into a big pothole, we do have other people standing by."
  • Yager, Craig-Hallum: asked about Chamonix/Bronco Billy’s improvements; CEO Lee cited revenue growth, cost controls, and specific operational changes, including, "It's Don Juan's now" for the revamped restaurant and "we have seven people" focused on hotel group sales to build future bookings.
  • Chad Beynon, Macquarie: asked about M&A appetite; CEO Lee said, "we're pretty busy" and "We're pretty heavily levered," adding, "we certainly don't want to issue equity at these prices," while President Fanger said, "If this conversation were three years later... it'd be a different answer from us."
  • Beynon, Macquarie: asked about American Place flow-through; CEO Lee said the property is showing "very, very steady growth" and highlighted capacity constraints as rationale for the permanent build, while President Fanger cited May performance: "$4.4 million of EBITDA" on "$12.7 million" of gaming revenue.
  • John DeCree, CBRE: asked about construction timing; CEO Lee reiterated "18 to 24 months" and said the company "probably will not release" a "$3 million" earthmoving contract "until we have the financing tied together."
  • DeCree, CBRE: asked about financing cost; President Fanger answered, "It is, I think, yes" (within expectations), and CEO Lee added, "Some components... might be in very low double digits" with a blend "hopefully still in single digits."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly negative to neutral around timing and leverage, shown by repeated financing timeline questions and cost-of-capital probing (e.g., DeCree seeking "all-in cost of financing" and Yager asking "what's your confidence").
  • Management tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks and more defensive-detail-oriented in Q&A, with CEO Lee emphasizing document complexity ("any sentence can screw you") and confidence hedges ("we're 95% sure we're going to get there").
  • Versus last quarter, management language moved from planning/legislative uncertainty to execution milestones, as President Fanger said the extension was granted and "we are now permitted to operate... until February of 2029," and management repeated an expectation to complete the refinancing "in the third quarter."

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • The temporary-casino extension progressed from "a bill was introduced" to extend operations (Q1) to "permitted... until February of 2029" with Gaming Board approval (Q2) (President Fanger).
  • Financing commentary shifted from Q1’s "potentially in the next few weeks" and expectation to "commence construction within the next few weeks" (President Fanger) to Q2’s emphasis on completion of the revolver commitments and expectation to finish "in the third quarter" amid extensive documentation (President Fanger; CEO Lee).
  • Chamonix messaging advanced from Q1’s negative property EBITDA ("minus $1.3 million") (President Fanger) to Q2’s "approximately break-even" result and a quantified EBITDA pathway tied to win-per-position goals (President Fanger).

Risks and Concerns

  • "It's a pretty complicated transaction" with "1,500 pages of documents" (President Fanger; CEO Lee), and CEO Lee said inter-creditor issues can slow timelines as "lawyers like to play ping-pong."
  • Operational disruptions included "a 42-hour power outage" at Rising Star (President Fanger) and ongoing Grand Lodge headwinds as renovations "continue to disrupt our casino business in the near term" (President Fanger).
  • Chamonix execution risk was framed through underperformance versus market benchmarks: "At Chamonix, we're currently at about half the Black Hawk average" in win per position per day (President Fanger).

Final Takeaway

Management emphasized that Q2 growth was driven by American Place’s record results and Chamonix’s marketing-led improvement to near break-even, while highlighting a concrete Illinois milestone that extends temporary operations to February 2029 and supports the plan to complete a multi-part refinancing in Q3. For Chamonix, management laid out explicit performance benchmarks—raising win per position per day from about $175 toward the Black Hawk average—as the pathway to roughly $30 million to $40 million of annual EBITDA over time, while reiterating an 18-to-24-month construction timeline for the permanent American Place, with an opening target around Q3 2028.

data.title: Rising Treasury yields could pressure equity valuations, Fidelity's Timmer says
data.description:
Rising U.S. Treasury yields could weigh on equity valuations as bonds become more competitive with stocks, Fidelity Global Macro Director Jurrien Timmer said, pointing to historical market relationships.

Timmer said that when risk-free assets offered returns comparable to equities, higher Treasury yields had historically coincided with lower equity valuations.

He said that the relationship prevailed from the 1960s through the mid-1990s and warned that risky assets could face severe consequences if they ignored it, citing the 1987 stock market crash as an example.

A chart shared by Timmer compared the price-to-earnings ratios of the 10-year U.S. Treasury and the S&P 500 over more than six decades. It highlighted a period of positive stock-bond correlation from the late 1960s through the early 2000s, followed by a prolonged period of negative correlation.

The chart also tracked the so-called Fed Model, the gap between bond and equity valuation multiples, which turned positive again lately and stood at about 15% in the latest reading. According to the chart, the S&P 500's trailing operating earnings price-to-earnings ratio was 24.4, compared with 21.1 for the 10-year Treasury.

Timmer said the recent rise in Treasury yields had made risk-free assets increasingly competitive with equities, reviving a relationship that had largely faded during the low-interest-rate era. He said a further repricing in Treasury valuations could also put pressure on equity valuations.
